Earthquake-resistant building design incorporates three (3) fundamental strategies: (1) increasing structural strength (brute-force resistance), (2) improving ductility (the capacity to deform without failure), and (3) implementing base isolation (decoupling the structure from ground motion). Modern building codes (e.g., IBC, International Building Code) specify minimum requirements based on seismic zone classification and occupancy category. Base isolation systems typically use elastomeric bearings (natural or synthetic rubber with lead cores, abbreviated LRB) or friction pendulum bearings (FPB). These reduce spectral acceleration by a factor of 3-5x compared to fixed-base structures. Damping devices (viscous, friction, or tuned mass dampers, i.e., TMDs) provide supplemental energy dissipation. Instrumentation is essential: accelerometers placed at foundation, mid-height, and roof levels enable real-time structural health monitoring (SHM). Post-earthquake assessment follows the ATC-20 tagging protocol (green = inspected, yellow = restricted use, red = unsafe). Cost premium for seismic design typically ranges from 1-5% of total construction cost (a modest investment relative to potential loss).
